name: Radiation pressure
seoTitle: Radiation pressure Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Radiation pressure: work out luminosity from the angle and the distance. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Radiation pressure calculator turns the angle, the distance and the pressure into luminosity. That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Radiation pressure calculator work?
sections.html:
The Radiation pressure calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports luminosity in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of surface); then you type in the angle, the distance, the pressure (Pressure outside the Sun) and the pressure (Pressure inside the Sun).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as opaque and reflective. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in degrees. The unit chip switches it to any of the 12 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in astronomical units. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in micropascals. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in gigapascals. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Radiation pressure calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Luminosity=1199169832 × PI × (distance ^ 2) × pressure ÷ (type of surface × (the cosine of (angle), 2))
Temperature=(100000 ÷ 687797) × the square root of (110) × (3 ^ 1 ÷ 4) × (62527 ^ 3 ÷ 4) × (pressure ^ 1 ÷ 4)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in solar luminosities, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kelvins, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Power, opening in solar luminosities
  • Length, opening in astronomical units
  • Pressure, opening in micropascals
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Pressure, opening in gigapascals

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Radiation pressure calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the angle, the distance and the pressure — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Radiation pressure calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns luminosity, derived from the angle, the distance and the pressure. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Radiation pressure calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the angle, the distance and the pressure, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter angle in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Angle opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Radiation pressure calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
